title: Lumbosacral Spondylolisthesis(Archived) -- Introduction
content: Lumbosacral spondylolisthesis is the forward translation of the fifth lumbar vertebra (L5) over the first sacral vertebra (S1). Bilateral L5 pars defect (spondylolysis) or repetitive stress injury is the primary etiology behind lumbosacral spondylolisthesis. The degree of a slip often correlates with the degree of symptoms.

title: Lumbosacral Spondylolisthesis(Archived) -- Introduction
content: The most commonly affected populations are children and adolescents participating in sports that require repetitive lower back hyperextension (divers, pace cricket bowlers, baseball, softball, rugby, weightlifting, sailing, table tennis, wrestlers, gymnasts, dancers, and footballers). They typically present with lower back pain that is exacerbated by activity. [2] Occasionally, pain can radiate to both buttocks and legs, and in advanced cases, the gait pattern and walking distance may be affected. Presentation in adults is more insidious and commonly associated with long-standing degenerative changes secondary to the slip, often leading to spinal canal stenosis and radicular pain. Management of the majority of the cases is non-operative, but patients who fail non-operative treatment and continue having disabling symptoms may require surgical treatment. [2] [3]

title: Lumbosacral Spondylolisthesis(Archived) -- Etiology
content: A Wiltse-Newman classification describes different etiologies of pars interarticularis failure: Type I  Dysplastic – congenital defect in the pars Type II (isthmic) is the most common II A pars fatigue fracture II B pars elongation due to multiple healed stress fractures II C pars acute fracture Type III degenerative spondylolisthesis from degenerative facet instability without pars fracture Type IV Traumatic – due to acute posterior arch fracture other than the pars Type V  Neoplastic – pathologic destruction of the pars [4] Depending on the degree of the forward slip, the severity of this process is graded as mild, severe, or complete slip (spondyloptosis) - described later in the Myerding classification. In the most common type of isthmic spondylolisthesis, which leads to a L5/S1 slip, the following stages have been identified.

title: Lumbosacral Spondylolisthesis(Archived) -- Etiology
content: The second most common types of spondylolisthesis are type I (dysplastic) and III (degenerative). Degenerative spondylolisthesis is most prevalent in the adult population, with the L4/L5 level being affected most frequently, followed by the L3/L4 level. Due to the chronicity of the instability, degenerative changes often associated with the intervertebral disc and facet joints frequently occur. They often lead to secondary hypertrophy of the ligamentum flavum, resulting in subsequent spinal canal stenosis. This condition usually presents with bilateral buttock pain and neurogenic claudication (back pain eased by sitting down/leaning forward).

title: Lumbosacral Spondylolisthesis(Archived) -- Epidemiology
content: Estimates are that 4 to 6% of the population has a degree of lumbosacral spondylolisthesis. The majority of cases are asymptomatic. [5] Most of the symptomatic high-grade slips occur in the pediatric/adolescent population participating in sports involving repetitive hyperextension. At the same time, adults tend to present with milder and more chronic onset of symptoms. [6]

title: Lumbosacral Spondylolisthesis(Archived) -- Pathophysiology
content: Two mechanisms may cause the lytic defect. The first is the pincer effect due to repeated hyperextension. [8] The inferior facet of L4 and the superior facet of S1 create a pincer effect on the pars interarticularis, causing a failure of the L5 pars. This condition is more likely to occur in a situation where the sacral slope has a low value with a more horizontally orientated superior sacral endplate. The second mechanism occurs when there is an increased sacral slope, resulting in increased traction on the pars interarticularis. [9] The repeated traction on the pars from a downsloping lumbosacral junction results in failure and fracture of the pars interarticularis. In high-grade slips, the anterosuperior part of the sacrum becomes dome-shaped, which may be due to repeated trauma to the anterosuperior apophyseal ring of the S1 vertebrae. [10]

title: Lumbosacral Spondylolisthesis(Archived) -- Pathophysiology
content: Pelvic Tilt (PT) is the angle measured between a line drawn from the center of the superior endplate of S1 to the center of rotation of the femoral head and the vertical reference line. [11]

title: Lumbosacral Spondylolisthesis(Archived) -- Pathophysiology
content: Sacral Slope (SS) is the angle between the line drawn along the superior end of the S1 endplate and the horizontal reference line. [11] The pelvic tilt (PT) and sacral slope are referenced to the vertical and horizontal planes, and therefore can vary depending on the position of the pelvis. Although the standard measurements are taken on a standing radiograph, the values of PT and SS vary between sitting and standing positions.

title: Lumbosacral Spondylolisthesis(Archived) -- Pathophysiology
content: The Pelvic Incidence (PI) is the angle between a line starting at the midline between centers of rotation of each femoral head drawn towards the midpoint of S1 superior endplate and a line perpendicular to the line drawn along the superior endplate of S1.[10]  The normal value is 50 degrees. An increased Pelvic Incidence (PI) is associated with higher severity of slips. [12] In comparison to the PT and SS, the Pelvic Incidence is a fixed value and does not change with the position of the pelvis or in adult life. A value of 70 to 80 degrees is present in patients with significant spondylolisthesis. Pelvic Incidence = Pelvic Tilt + Sacral Slope

title: Lumbosacral Spondylolisthesis(Archived) -- Pathophysiology
content: Boxall’s Slip Angle and Dubosset’s lumbosacral angle measure the relationship between L5 and S1. [13] [14] The Boxalls slip angle is measured between the perpendicular to the posterior aspect of the S1 vertebrae and the lower border of L5. If the slip angle measures greater than 45 degrees, it is associated with a higher risk of slip progression, instability, and postoperative pseudoarthrosis. It predicts intervention and affects cosmesis as well as prognosis. [11] The Dubosset’s lumbosacral angle is measured between the posterior aspect of the S1 and the upper endplate of the L5. Unlike the slip angle, the lumbosacral angle does not involve surfaces that alter with dysplasia.

title: Lumbosacral Spondylolisthesis(Archived) -- Pathophysiology
content: Forward translation of the vertebrae may cause a narrowing of the spinal canal at the level of the slip. This situation is rare, as most slips are only grade I or II; however, secondary canal and foraminal stenosis can occur due to subsequent degenerative changes in facet joints, hypertrophy of the ligamentum flavum, hypertrophic fibrous repair tissue of the pars defect, or bulging of the L5/S1 disc. In severe L5/S1 slips, the L5 nerve root is most commonly affected by being pulled forward by the superior vertebra.

title: Lumbosacral Spondylolisthesis(Archived) -- History and Physical -- History
content: Children participating in back hyperextension activities (such as gymnastics, football, and weightlifting) typically present at the most common age of 4 to 6 years old. In adults, the insidious onset of axial back pain is exacerbated by physical activity, with periodic exacerbations that vary in intensity and duration. L5 radicular symptoms (in severe slips), including weakness of the extensor hallucis longus Bladder and bowel dysfunction (including cauda equina syndrome in extreme cases) Neurologic claudication secondary to spinal canal stenosis (buttock and leg pain worse with walking but improving with leaning forward or sitting)

title: Lumbosacral Spondylolisthesis(Archived) -- History and Physical -- Examination Findings
content: Pain with back hyperextension. Hyperextending the lower back while standing on 1 leg is termed the "stork test." Limitations of lumbar spine flexion and extension Increased popliteal angle Gait alteration with abductor weakness (L5) (pelvic waddle) Flattened lumbar lordosis or kyphosis of the lumbosacral junction Palpable step-off of the spinous process Hamstring tightness (in extreme cases, walking with hips and knees flexed- due to vertical orientation of the sacrum, causing pelvic retroversion and compensatory lumbar hyperlordosis + shortened stride and lurched posture) "Heart-shaped" buttocks in severe cases of significant lumbosacral kyphosis and sacral retroversion (sacrum becoming more vertical in orientation and moving away from the head of the femurs). The straight leg raise test may be positive. Scoliosis may be present, which could be secondary to pain.

title: Lumbosacral Spondylolisthesis(Archived) -- Evaluation
content: Following the history and examination, the best screening tool is an AP and lateral weight-bearing X-ray of the lumbar spine. [15]  Lumbosacral spondylolisthesis can be best assessed mainly on the lateral view, but occasional coronal deformity should not be missed. In cases where a clinical examination indicates an abnormal sagittal balance of the spinal column, a whole-spine lateral standing X-ray is indicated. In the majority of cases, an isthmic defect is detected on radiographs; however, in cases of doubt, an MRI scan is recommended for further evaluation. Oblique X-rays of the lumbosacral junction, Computerized Tomography (CT) scans, and SPECT scans may also help identify the defect; however, they involve exposure to ionizing radiation.

title: Lumbosacral Spondylolisthesis(Archived) -- Evaluation
content: MRI scans are more sensitive in identifying pars lesions.MRI can also identify stress reactions that occur even before a fracture line develops. [16] In dysplastic cases, a dome-shaped or significantly inclined sacrum can present, as well as trapezoid-shaped L5 and dysplastic facets of S1. Neoplasms and infections are an extremely rare primary cause of spondylolisthesis, but should merit consideration as a differential diagnosis in patients with constitutional symptoms. To assess dynamic instability, flexion and extension views should be obtained. Either 4 mm of translation or 10 degrees of angulation of motion compared to the adjacent motion segment is diagnostic for spondylolisthesis. Grading of the forward slip is classified by the Meyerding classification: Grade I <25% of the width of the vertebra on the lateral view Grade II 25 to 50% Grade III 50 to 75% Grade IV 75 to 100% Grade V >100% (spondyloptosis) Pelvic incidence (PI) has a direct correlation to Meyerding's grade. [12]

title: Lumbosacral Spondylolisthesis(Archived) -- Evaluation
content: The Spinal Deformity Study Group has created a new classification that guides treatment. This scale takes into account the spinopelvic parameters and the overall spinal alignment. [17] I < 50% slip, PI < 45 degrees; surgery only if non-operative methods do not control symptoms. II < 50% slip, PI 45 to 60, Surgery only if non-operative methods do not control symptoms. III < 50% slip, PI >60 degrees, posterolateral fusion can be considered IV >50% slip, balanced pelvis high SS / low PT, decompression + / - Posterolateral fusion may be adequate V >50% slip, Unbalanced pelvis (retroverted), Low SS / High PT, reduction of slip, and circumferential fusion may be a consideration. VI >50% slip, Unbalanced spine (retroverted pelvis), Low SS / High PT + C7 plumbline anterior to femoral heads, reduction of slip and circumferential fusion may be considered.

title: Lumbosacral Spondylolisthesis(Archived) -- Evaluation
content: MRI (T2-weighted sequence) is best for assessing spinal canal stenosis, foraminal stenosis, and nerve root impingement, as well as the morphology of lumbar and sacral vertebrae. The presence of these findings, correlated with a history and examination, dictates the surgical management. The most commonly affected nerve root is the L5 nerve root.

title: Lumbosacral Spondylolisthesis(Archived) -- Treatment / Management
content: The majority of the cases can be treated non-operatively by: Thoracolumbosacral / lumbosacral brace. [18] In acute cases of adolescent sportspersons, bracing to prevent extension is shown to be superior to activity modification alone. Activity modification (avoidance of hyperextension) [19] Core muscles strengthening, focusing on the deep abdominal muscles and the multifidus muscle [20] Lumbar flexion-based exercises. [21] Analgesia In cases of adult degenerative spondylolisthesis with canal stenosis, an epidural steroid injection can provide short-term relief. [22]

title: Lumbosacral Spondylolisthesis(Archived) -- Treatment / Management

Among those treated non-operatively, 82% returned to their previous level of play. [19] Approximately one-third of patients with spondylolisthesis experience a disease progression over time. Operative treatment is reserved for those with intractable pain or neurological symptoms, including claudication or radiculopathy. title: Lumbosacral Spondylolisthesis(Archived) -- Treatment / Management
content: Anterior/posterior/transforaminal and direct lateral lumbosacral interbody fusion, reduction, and fusion. [28] The anterior, posterior, transforaminal, and direct lateral indicate the path through which the interbody device or cage is inserted. Posterior lumbar interbody fusion (PLIF) involves the insertion of the cage between the vertebral bodies medial to the facets. Transforaminal lumbar interbody fusion (TLIF) requires facetectomy and a more lateralized and transforaminal approach to the disc space. Anterior Lumbar Interbody Fusion (ALIF) is performed via a transperitoneal or retroperitoneal approach, offering better access to the disc space and endplate. They can also be associated with retrograde ejaculation and sexual dysfunction. The direct lateral or transpsoas approach can only access the disc spaces above the L5 vertebrae. The iliac crest is in the path of reaching the L5/S1 disc on the direct lateral approach. [29]

title: Lumbosacral Spondylolisthesis(Archived) -- Treatment / Management
content: Reduction with spondylectomy (vertebrectomy) of L5 and fusion of L4 on S1. [30] In severe slips, removing the L5 vertebrae allows reduction and better spinal alignment.

title: Lumbosacral Spondylolisthesis(Archived) -- Treatment / Management
content: Operative options should be considered only if non-operative options fail or symptoms are significant. The reduction of the slip is controversial, as it causes L5 nerve root injury in approximately 20% of cases. Nevertheless, some evidence suggests that patients who undergo reduction and instrumented fusion may experience better functional and cosmetic outcomes. [32] Foraminal decompression may also be necessary. Interbody fusion with the maintenance of intervertebral space improves the foraminal height, helps restore lumbar lordosis, and avoids fusion to L4 in high-grade slips. Each case requires an individualized approach, and factors such as the degree of spondylolisthesis, predominant neurological symptoms, and the patient's comorbidities should be taken into consideration. [33] Minimally invasive surgical techniques are gaining in popularity. [34]

title: Lumbosacral Spondylolisthesis(Archived) -- Differential Diagnosis
content: The differential diagnoses for Lumbosacral Spondylolisthesis include the following: Mechanical or muscular back pain Disc degeneration, facet joint osteoarthritis (OA), and/or cyst Lumbar canal stenosis secondary to degenerative changes Neoplastic process/metastases Infection (discitis, TB, paraspinal abscess) Vascular claudication (improves at rest in a standing position while neurological claudication improves with lumbar spine flexion - leaning forward or sitting)

title: Lumbosacral Spondylolisthesis(Archived) -- Prognosis
content: Despite the estimate of up to 6% of the population suffering from spondylolisthesis, the majority of them are asymptomatic. Only a small percentage of symptomatic cases will require surgical treatment. The majority of the worst prognoses occur in cases of: Very young age at presentation Female Slip angle >45 degrees High-grade slip Degenerative slip (most commonly in adults)

title: Lumbosacral Spondylolisthesis(Archived) -- Complications
content: The complications that can manifest with Lumbosacral Spondylolisthesis are as follows: The most common reported neurological complication after lumbosacral spondylolisthesis surgery is L5 nerve root dysfunction. It is most frequently associated with high-grade slips and attempts at slip reduction as well as foraminal stenosis decompression. L5 nerve root dysfunction is usually transient and resolves within a few months in the postoperative period. In their cadaveric study, Petraco et al found that 71% of total nerve strain occurs during the second half of the reduction. [35] Pseudoarthrosis Dural tear Adjacent segment disease (2 to 3%) Surgical site infection (0.1 to 2%) Positioning neuropathy: Lateral femoral cutaneous nerve - from a prone position with iliac bolster, ulnar nerve, or brachial plexopathy with inappropriate arm position. [36] The complication rate increases with age, increased intraoperative blood loss, longer operative times, and the number of levels fused.

title: Lumbosacral Spondylolisthesis(Archived) -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: Sports coaches and personal trainers working with children and adolescents, especially those involved in gymnastics, football, or weightlifting, should be aware of the symptoms of spondylosis and spondylolisthesis. They should be able to identify cases when pain does not improve after rest and basic stretching and strengthening exercises. These athletes need to be referred for specialist evaluation to diagnose and treat their conditions. This is particularly important as braces that prevent extension and activity reduction have shown excellent results.

title: Lumbosacral Spondylolisthesis(Archived) -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: Affected patients should be educated about the importance of modifying their activities and engaging in physiotherapy, as well as core muscle strengthening and flexion exercises, for symptomatic treatment. They should receive reassurance that most of the symptoms are transient. But at the same time, especially those with a high risk of slip progression should be followed up by a specialist Orthopedic surgeon and educated about symptoms and signs of slip progression and potentially serious complications like cauda equina syndrome.

title: Lumbosacral Spondylolisthesis(Archived) -- Pearls and Other Issues
content: Pars interarticularis defects were common in athletes involved in high-activity sports. Hyperextension of the spine during the sport was a risk factor. In cricket, fast bowlers extended and laterally flexed their spines before throwing the ball to increase the speed of delivery. This repetitive movement increased the likelihood of developing a pars defect. In a recent review pars interarticularis defects were more common in the following sports, diving (35.38%), cricket (31.97%), baseball/softball (26.91%), rugby (22.22%), weightlifting (19.49%), sailing (17.18%), table tennis (15.63%), and wrestling (14.74%). [19] The suspicion that young adolescent sportspersons could develop spondylolysis is crucial in early diagnosis and prevention of progression. Bracing and activity restriction have shown excellent results with a good return to the same level of play.

title: Lumbosacral Spondylolisthesis(Archived) -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: A high level of suspicion is needed among sports coaches, general practitioners, and parents to recognize patients with symptoms of spondylolisthesis. Groups at risk, such as adolescent gymnasts, football players, and weightlifters, should undergo regular health screening checks. Those with a history of lower back pain associated with these activities should undergo further evaluation and examination. Individuals with suggestive signs and symptoms should undergo radiological investigations.
